SD-2026-HB1001.s: This law lets a person who owns land next to state-owned land bordering the Missouri River ask to use prescribed burning on the state land with written consent from the official in charge. The request must say the burn is for controlling woody species and managing grassland, describe the land, and give the time for the burn. A person who gets consent must provide fire suppression resources, follow other laws, and takes all liability for the burn. The state is immune from liability for a prescribed burn done under this law.

SD-2026-HB1003.s: This law changes rules for criminal background checks for certain school employees. It keeps the fingerprint-based check for new hires, lets a person start work temporarily while results are pending, and allows results from a student teacher check to be used by other accredited schools. It also says an employee who works for more than one accredited school only needs one background investigation if it was done within the last five years, and it keeps bans on employment for people convicted of certain crimes.

SD-2026-HB1006.s: This law creates the Indian Medicaid Managed Care Model taskforce to study creating Indian medicaid managed care entities in South Dakota. The taskforce includes representatives from federally recognized Indian tribes, state agencies, lawmakers, a federal Indian Affairs representative, and members from the health care field. It will gather input from agencies, tribal representatives, health care industry representatives, and other stakeholders, then report findings, recommendations, and any proposed legislation to the Governor by December 1, 2028.

SD-2026-HB1007.s: This law changes the definition of "law enforcement officer" in South Dakota. It adds tribal law enforcement officers who are helping enforce state criminal or highway traffic laws, or helping prevent, detect, or prosecute crimes committed in the state. The change affects how the term is used in state law.

SD-2026-HB1012.s: This law revises and repeals rules about probation for contempt of a custody or visitation decree. It amends one section and repeals two others in South Dakota law. It affects people subject to custody or visitation decree contempt proceedings.

SD-2026-HB1013.s: This law sets the reasons certain offenders may be allowed to drive after a license revocation or driving-privilege suspension. The allowed reasons are employment, child care delivery or pickup, health appointments, school, court, probation appointments, 24/7 sobriety testing, counseling programs, treatment, or aftercare. It also requires proof of financial responsibility before driving and requires the person to keep that coverage during the restriction.

SD-2026-HB1014.s: This law changes the court surcharge rules for the first response in certain circuit court cases. It says the surcharge may not be collected in forcible entry and detainer actions, or when the responding party is the state, a county, a municipality, a school district, or a person receiving assistance benefits under title 28.

SD-2026-HB1017.s: This law lets a school board assign a student to an alternative setting for aggressive or violent behavior that disrupts school or affects health or safety. School districts must report those students to the Department of Education each year. The department may share the report only in anonymized, grouped form.

SD-2026-HB1018.s: This act changes the date when money appropriated to the Department of Education for improving and renovating the Cultural Heritage Center must be spent or obligated before it reverts. Any unused or unobligated amount by that date must revert under state procedures. The act was signed by the Governor.

SD-2026-HB1019.s: This law lets the secretary cancel a pesticide registration after a hearing if the pesticide or its labeling does not follow state law or rules, or if it is adulterated or misbranded. It affects registered pesticides and the people or companies that hold those registrations. The act was signed by the Governor.

SD-2026-HB1020.s: This law increases the maximum livestock ownership inspection fee that the board may set, from up to one dollar and sixty-five cents per head of livestock. It also keeps the board’s authority to set other brand and livestock fees and rules. The law applies to livestock owners and others covered by the state’s brand and inspection rules. An emergency is declared, so it takes effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-HB1022.s: This law changes how the department handles claims for victims' compensation. It requires the department to review and investigate properly filed claims, issue an order with certain findings and payment information, and send notice to the claimant. It also repeals one section of the crime victims' compensation law.

SD-2026-HB1027.s: This law updates South Dakota law to match current federal pipeline safety inspection citations. It adopts federal safety standards for gas pipelines and directs the Public Utilities Commission to run and enforce a pipeline safety inspection program. It also lets the commission make safety rules, work with the federal Department of Transportation when authorized, and keep certain trade secret information confidential.

SD-2026-HB1030.s: This act changes rules for when municipal elections are held in South Dakota. It lets some questions about municipal changes be put on the next regular municipal election if a petition is filed early enough, and it updates timing for special elections on matters like annexation, dissolution, and changing the form of government. It also allows some municipalities to move regular municipal elections to even-numbered years and makes related term and vacancy rules fit that schedule.

SD-2026-HB1034.s: This act adds extra fees when decals or license plates are mailed to vehicle owners or dealers. It also sets a mailing fee for a permit for vehicles used in the harvest of agricultural products. The higher fees apply to people and dealers who ask for mailed or express-mailed items.

SD-2026-HB1035.s: This law changes the rules for getting and keeping a public accountant license in South Dakota. It updates the board’s rulemaking powers, exam and education requirements, and the experience needed for a certificate. It also sets rules for applicants from other states and foreign jurisdictions, and for out-of-state accountants who want practice privileges in the state.

SD-2026-HB1038.s: This law lets the Public Utilities Commission assess actual costs when handling requests for electric service agreements for a data center customer of a public utility. It applies to data centers with a peak demand of 10 megawatts or greater, and the money collected goes to the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission gross receipts tax fund.

SD-2026-HB1040.s: This bill would revise South Dakota’s child support obligation schedule. It would keep using both parents’ combined monthly net incomes to set child support, with the noncustodial parent paying a share based on income. The bill also includes a self-support reserve and says a noncustodial parent who is incarcerated for more than 180 days must still owe at least the minimum base obligation.

SD-2026-HB1043.s: This law gives money from the general fund to the Department of Health to reimburse certain health care professionals. It covers four family physicians, two physician assistants, six nurse practitioners, and other eligible health care professionals who met the listed requirements. It also declares an emergency, so it takes effect right away.

SD-2026-HB1045.s: This law revises several child support rules. It changes how a court can set or adjust child support, including rules about imputed income, reasons to deviate from the support schedule, and when older support orders may be modified without showing a change in circumstances. It also changes how arrearages may be credited when a parent had primary physical custody for more than four straight months, and it updates hearing and notice procedures in child support cases.

SD-2026-HB1046.s: This law lets the Department of Corrections demolish the Pierre Minimum Center in Pierre, South Dakota. It also gives $682,825 from the general fund for that work, including removing fixtures and structures, abating hazardous materials, and restoring the site to grade.

SD-2026-HB1048.s: This law makes an appropriation of $87,000,000 in federal fund expenditure authority to the Governor's Office of Economic Development. The money is for grants to expand broadband infrastructure in South Dakota under the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program. It also declares an emergency, so it takes effect when approved.

SD-2026-HB1049.s: This law says certain “prohibited persons” may not control, operate, or own electric facilities in South Dakota, in whole or in part. It also bars agreements that give a prohibited person direct or indirect control of an electric facility, and any interest acquired in violation of the law must be divested within one year. The commission may investigate alleged violations and ask a court to enforce forfeiture, divestiture, or ending an illegal agreement.

SD-2026-HB1051.s: This law changes school district property tax levies and the formulas used to figure state aid for general education and special education. It sets new maximum school district levies for general fund taxes payable in 2027 and later, and it changes the special education levy and funding amounts. It also updates several education funding terms, including how fall enrollment, local need, local effort, and disability allocations are calculated.

SD-2026-HB1056.s: This law requires the Department of Social Services to ask the federal government for permission to exclude soft drinks from the supplemental nutrition assistance program. If the waiver is approved, the department must put the restriction in place within six months. If it is not approved, the secretary must keep submitting a waiver request every year until it is approved.

SD-2026-HB1062.s: This act revises South Dakota’s aggravated assault law. It says a person commits aggravated assault by causing or trying to cause serious bodily injury, using a dangerous weapon to cause or try to cause bodily injury, or assaulting someone in ways listed in the law. A person who violates the section is guilty of aggravated assault, which is a Class 3 felony.

SD-2026-HB1065.s: This law revises the medical purpose affirmative defense that can be used in cannabis prosecutions. It says the defense is presumed valid only if certain conditions are met, including a practitioner’s opinion, limits on the amount of cannabis, and secure storage for cultivation and extra cannabis. It also says a person is not required to have a registry identification card to raise that defense.

SD-2026-HB1066.s: This law revises the state rule on theft by a contractor, subcontractor, or supplier. It says a person who receives property for improving real estate and, with intent to defraud, uses it for something other than paying for labor, skill, or materials can be guilty of theft and punished under state law.

SD-2026-HB1067.s: This bill changes custody disputes between parents by creating a rebuttable presumption that joint physical custody is in the best interest of a minor child when either parent petitions for it. It defines joint physical custody as a division of time with the child that is approximately and reasonably equal for each parent. It also repeals a section that said nothing in the law creates a presumption of joint physical custody.

SD-2026-HB1073.s: This Act requires every public school and accredited nonpublic school to have a cardiac emergency response plan. The plan must include a response team, automated external defibrillators in accessible places, staff training in CPR and AED use, and procedures for sudden cardiac arrest or similar emergencies. Schools must review the plan, test and maintain defibrillators each year, and hold an annual drill, and the Department of Health gets $150,000 for grants to buy defibrillators.

SD-2026-HB1077.s: This measure would add cultivated-protein food products to the list of foods that are considered adulterated. It defines a cultivated-protein food product as a food made from manufacturing cells that resemble tissue from an agricultural food animal.

SD-2026-HB1080.s: This law lets a business owner who is a veteran apply for and display one set of military specialty plates on a noncommercial vehicle registered to the veteran's business. The veteran must be listed as an additional owner on the title, and the vehicle must be a noncommercial automobile, pickup truck, or van. It also says the business owner and veteran do not take on any additional liability from having the military specialty plates.

SD-2026-HB1082.s: This law says school districts may not charge students who are eligible for reduced-price meals through the National School Lunch Program or School Breakfast Program for meals served by the district through those programs. It also directs the Department of Education to calculate and reimburse school districts for the cost of those meals using money in the general appropriation bill. School districts and students who qualify for reduced-price meals are affected.

SD-2026-HB1084.s: This act changes what voter registration records and statewide and county voter file archives must be open to public inspection. It keeps certain personal information, like Social Security numbers, driver license numbers, and month and day of birth, from public view. It also hides home addresses, phone numbers, and personal email addresses for current or retired state or federal judges and justices and for law enforcement officers, while keeping their city and county of residence public.

SD-2026-HB1086.s: This bill would appropriate money from the general fund to the Department of Corrections for a grant to a nonprofit corporation. The nonprofit would have to offer trauma-informed programming with leadership development and personal and professional skills training at state correctional facilities, and it would need to serve offenders and correctional staff. The program would be for the South Dakota State Penitentiary, Mike Durfee State Prison, and South Dakota Women's Prison.

SD-2026-HB1089.s: This act changes how severance tax revenue from new precious metals permits is split between the state and counties. For permits issued on or after July 1, 2026, most of the revenue goes to the state general fund and the rest goes to the county where the metals were severed. It also says revenue from severing precious metals from state-owned or state-controlled land goes to the common school permanent fund.

SD-2026-HB1092.s: This act updates South Dakota's open records law by listing many kinds of records that are not subject to disclosure. The closed records include student, medical, personnel, law enforcement, security, emergency response, and certain financial and settlement records. It also keeps some library patron, donor, and personal identifying information confidential.

SD-2026-HB1095.s: This law changes the rules for nominating petitions for municipal, school board, and some primary election candidates in South Dakota. It sets filing deadlines, says what information must be on the petition, and gives rules for when petitions may be circulated. It also changes how candidates may withdraw and when an unopposed candidate may be certified or an election canceled.

SD-2026-HB1096.s: This law allows a limited liability limited partnership to be created directly by filing a certificate with the secretary of state. It also keeps a way for an existing limited partnership to qualify as a limited liability limited partnership. The certificate must include the partnership’s name, office address information, and a statement that it elects to be a limited liability limited partnership.

SD-2026-HB1098.s: This law changes how South Dakota funds special education in school districts. It sets new rules for the special education levy and updates the funding amounts for students with different disability levels. It also allows up to 15% of local need to be used for early intervening services for students in kindergarten through grade 12 who are not yet identified for special education but need extra help.

SD-2026-HB1099.s: This law changes South Dakota’s controlled substances list to except the pharmaceutical composition of crystalline polymorph psilocybin in a drug product approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration from Schedule I. It also amends the state list of hallucinogenic substances and other drugs covered in that section. The change affects drugs containing psilocybin that meet the FDA-approved drug product exception.

SD-2026-HB1102.s: This Act changes when certain entities must file annual reports in South Dakota. Most entities must file either in the month of the first-year anniversary of formation or by January thirty-first each year. Banks organized under the listed law and limited partnerships organized under chapter 48-7 are excepted, and the Act takes effect beginning January 1, 2027.

SD-2026-HB1104.s: This law revises the application requirements for special license plates and parking permits for people with substantial physical disabilities in South Dakota. It lets an eligible vehicle owner or a parent or legal guardian apply with a signed certification from certain licensed health care workers. It also keeps the rules for portable parking certificates that allow parking without a time limit and in spaces reserved for a person with a physical disability.

SD-2026-HB1105.s: This bill would stop property owners from using contracts or declarations to block healthcare services on commercial or residential property in medically underserved areas, communities, or counties with a medically underserved population. It applies to property in those areas and to agreements that try to restrict that use. It also says a contract or declaration that violates this rule is not enforceable.

SD-2026-HB1106.s: This law changes how county extension board members are appointed and how long they serve. It says the members must be appointed to staggered terms of one to three years, ending on January 10. The law applies to county boards that establish cooperative extension work and sets rules for who may serve on those boards.

SD-2026-HB1107.s: This law lets a court change or remove restrictions on land if changed conditions make it impossible or impractical to keep using the land as planned. The court may also allow the land to be sold, and the money must be reinvested in a way that fits the original public purpose. It applies to lands held for benevolent, charitable, educational, religious, or other public purposes.

SD-2026-HB1108.s: This law requires court files to be sealed in certain protection order cases when a petition is dismissed or denied. It covers petitions under two sections of South Dakota law and can require law enforcement to make related records nonpublic after a sealing order. The Unified Judicial System must apply some of these sealing rules retroactively to electronic court records.

SD-2026-HB1111.s: This act changes the rules for getting an agricultural processor's lien for people who own or lease and operate farm machinery to process a crop. It says the lien filing must include certain names, addresses, amounts, locations, and dates, and it must be filed electronically with the secretary of state. It also sets notice rules if the crop is sold or consigned, gives the lien priority if filed within sixty days, and says the lien must be enforced within sixty days after the financing statement is filed.

SD-2026-HB1118.s: This law lets the Board of Regents contract for the design, construction, furnishing, and equipping of an addition to the existing swine wean-to-finish barn at South Dakota State University. It appropriates $1,720,000 for the project and allows the Board of Regents to use donated money, federal money, or other outside money for it. The act also says the project is under the supervision of the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration and takes effect as an emergency measure.

SD-2026-HB1123.s: This act sets up a pilot program for people who receive temporary assistance for needy families. The Department of Social Services must provide monthly benefits for menstrual hygiene products for participants ages eighteen to fifty who experience menstruation, and for diapers for dependents under age three. The department must also give information on the benefits, make sure they are used only for the approved items, report to the Legislature by September 1, 2029, and use an appropriation of $2,500,000 from the general fund to fund the program.

SD-2026-HB1126.s: This act revises the rules for a sixth or later driving under the influence offense when the person has the required prior convictions within the listed time periods. It makes that offense an aggravated offense and a Class 4 felony, and it requires at least six years in a state correctional facility in some cases, plus a driver license revocation of at least three years. The person’s supervision must include at least one monitoring or treatment option, such as an alcohol or drug accountability program, an ignition interlock, a breath alcohol interlock, or an alcohol monitoring bracelet.

SD-2026-HB1130.s: This act changes what a school district may pay for from its capital outlay fund. It allows the fund to be used for items like land, facilities, improvements, installment and lease-purchase payments, property insurance premiums, transportation contract costs, warranties, textbooks, instructional software, and equipment. It also lets a school district move up to forty-five percent of the total tax revenues in that fund to the general fund during the current school fiscal year.

SD-2026-HB1134.s: This bill would appropriate $101 from the general fund to the state for the economic development prosperity of South Dakota. It would also require the state to approve vouchers and the state auditor to draw warrants to pay the allowed spending.

SD-2026-HB1135.s: The bill would appropriate $101 from the general fund to the state to enhance the economic health of South Dakota. It would require the state to approve vouchers and the state auditor to draw warrants for spending allowed by the act. Any money not lawfully spent or obligated would revert under state law.

SD-2026-HB1136.s: This bill would appropriate $101 from the general fund to the state for developing South Dakota. The state would approve vouchers and the state auditor would draw warrants to pay the spending allowed under the act, and any unused money would revert under state law.

SD-2026-HB1137.s: This act gives the Board of Regents $40,000,000 to plan and build an athletic facility at the University of South Dakota. The facility may include an indoor track, practice areas, locker rooms, offices, meeting rooms, training and nutrition space, ticketing and concession areas, restrooms, elevators, suites, and seating for two thousand spectators. The act also allows other money from federal sources, donations, or other sources to be used for the project. It takes effect at once because an emergency is declared.

SD-2026-HB1138.s: The bill would require non-medical home care agencies to get a license from the Department of Health before operating in South Dakota. It would set rules for agency owners and home care aides, including training, criminal history background checks, record keeping, and professional liability insurance. It would also let the department inspect agencies and deny, suspend, or revoke a license for violations.

SD-2026-HB1139.s: This bill would appropriate money for the ordinary expenses of the legislative, judicial, and executive departments of state government, the current expenses of state institutions, interest on the public debt, and common schools. It also sets funding levels and budget changes for several state agencies and programs, including the Office of the Governor, the Bureau of Finance and Management, the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration, and the Bureau of Information and Technology. The act applies to the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027.

SD-2026-HB1140.s: This law lets a court require a defendant on probation to take part in and finish a program at a nonprofit entity that received an alternative care program grant, if the defendant agrees, the program has room, and the application is approved before sentencing. It also lets a court, in certain cases, use that kind of program as a condition of parole. The law also lets a court allow limited driving after a court-approved chemical dependency counseling program and proof of financial responsibility, including for attendance at treatment or an alternative care program.

SD-2026-HB1143.s: This law lets a student with asthma, anaphylaxis, or diabetes possess and self-administer certain prescription medication on school property or at a school-related event or activity. The student must have a diagnosis from a licensed health care provider and the parent and provider must give written authorization and other required statements to the school. The school must keep the provider’s statement in the student’s educational record.

SD-2026-HB1146.s: This law adopts the physician assistant licensure compact in South Dakota. It lets physician assistants with a qualifying license in one participating state apply to practice in other participating states under a compact privilege. The law also sets rules for license checks, background checks, complaints, and discipline, and it keeps a state’s licensing board in charge of action against licenses it issues.

SD-2026-HB1147.s: This bill would appropriate $5,000,000 from the general fund to the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources. The department would give one grant to a South Dakota-based statewide food distribution organization that serves all counties, for buying food and distributing it to food pantries across the state. At least $1,500,000 of the grant would have to be used to buy food from local farmers and other eligible producers in South Dakota.

SD-2026-HB1148.s: This law adopts the respiratory care interstate compact. It lets respiratory therapists licensed in one member state practice in other member states under a compact privilege, if they meet the compact’s requirements. It also requires applicants for respiratory care licensure to submit fingerprints for state and federal criminal background checks. The law includes special provisions for active military members and their spouses.

SD-2026-HB1149.s: This law adopts the Athletic Trainer Licensure Compact in South Dakota. It lets qualified licensed athletic trainers practice in other member states under a compact privilege, and it keeps state licensing rules in place. Athletic trainers who seek to join the compact must complete a fingerprint-based criminal background check and pay the cost of fingerprinting and the check.

SD-2026-HB1160.s: This bill would repeal the medical marijuana oversight committee in South Dakota law. It would also remove the committee’s duties to meet, review the medical cannabis program, and make recommendations to the Legislature and the department. The repeal would affect the committee, its members, and the medical cannabis program it reviews.

SD-2026-HB1164.s: This law makes it a Class 5 felony for a licensed health care provider to use a donor's reproductive material without the patient's written consent, or to use the provider's own reproductive material without that consent, during an assisted reproduction procedure. It also lets certain people, including the patient, spouse, intended parent, child, or donor, bring a civil lawsuit for a violation. A person who wins such a case can receive damages, attorney's fees, and, in some cases, the costs of the procedure.

SD-2026-HB1168.s: This bill would let a property owner get a property tax credit for nonpublic school tuition paid for a child who is at least five years old but younger than nineteen and enrolled in a kindergarten-through-twelfth-grade nonpublic school in this state. The child does not have to be the owner’s child. The credit would be limited to the lesser of eighty percent of the school district taxes owed or one thousand dollars, and the owner would have to apply by June first with school enrollment information and tuition verification.

SD-2026-HB1169.s: This law classifies medetomidine as a Schedule III controlled substance in South Dakota. It allows certain animal uses, including approved or permissible dispensing, prescribing, administering, manufacturing, distributing, or using medetomidine under federal law, and use of medetomidine bulk chemical for pharmaceutical compounding by a licensed pharmacist or veterinarian.

SD-2026-HB1173.s: This bill changes how the Public Utilities Commission handles permit applications. It says certain applicants must prepare and pay for an environmental impact statement, and the commission may require one in other cases. The bill also changes the fees that may be charged and says the rules apply to pending and future permit applications before the commission.

SD-2026-HB1175.s: This law lets the Division of Criminal Investigation do national criminal history checks for people seeking or holding certain tribal positions, but only when an Indian tribe asks for it. The listed positions include tribal council members, tribal judges, tribal board or commission members, conservation officers, tribal education staff, child protection and youth program workers, juvenile offender workers, gaming licensees, and foster or adoptive parents. The tribe, or the applicant if the tribe requires it, must pay the processing fees.

SD-2026-HB1176.s: The bill would let a court make bond or pre-trial release depend on participation in the 24/7 sobriety program and payment of related costs. It says a defendant could not be jailed, or have bond or pre-trial release revoked, for failing to pay unless the court finds the defendant has the present and continued ability to pay. It also keeps the 24/7 sobriety fund in the state treasury to help pay program costs and reimburse counties in some cases.

SD-2026-HB1179.s: This bill would change the reimbursement fee paid to a garnishee for preparing a garnishment disclosure from fifteen dollars to forty dollars. The fee would still be taxed as part of the plaintiff's costs. If the garnishee is not paid, the garnishment proceeding is void.

SD-2026-HB1180.s: This law lets owners of a jointly owned business agree to a non-compete term in the business documents or in a purchase, sale, or transfer contract. After an owner transfers their interest, the agreement may stop them from doing the same or similar business in the business’s area for up to three years. It applies to owners in jointly owned business entities.

SD-2026-HB1183.s: This act revises who can get immunity from arrest, charge, or prosecution after a drug-related overdose. A person who has an overdose and needs medical help may be covered if they or another person contact law enforcement or emergency medical services to request help. The immunity applies only when the evidence for the charge was obtained because of the overdose and the need for medical assistance.

SD-2026-HB1184.s: This act defines terms like “man,” “woman,” “male,” “female,” “boy,” “girl,” “father,” and “mother” in state law. It says those definitions apply across state administrative rules, contracts, guidance documents, policies, practices, statutes, and political subdivisions. It also directs state agencies, departments, boards, commissions, institutions, and other entities using state authority to follow those definitions.

SD-2026-HB1187.s: This law adds coaches of school activities to the list of people who must report suspected child abuse or neglect. It affects coaches and other mandatory reporters who have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect of a child under 18.

SD-2026-HB1188.s: This act lets certain state and local officers, and people working for them, arrange to remove a disabled vehicle from a highway, right of way, or public waters when it cannot be moved quickly by the driver or person in charge. It also lets them remove spilled cargo or other property that could block traffic or create a safety hazard. The owner must pay the removal costs. Unless there is gross negligence or willful and wanton misconduct, these officers and removal workers are not liable for damage to the vehicle, cargo, personal property, or the surrounding area.

SD-2026-HB1189.s: This law raises the tire weight limit for a mobile crane moving on a highway in South Dakota when it is operating under a permit. It also keeps the existing tire weight limits for other types of axles and says a violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor.

SD-2026-HB1193.s: This law changes property tax relief rules for disabled veterans and surviving spouses. It lets eligible people get a refund or abatement of taxes if they missed the application deadline, and in some cases the refund can go back up to four years. It also keeps the exemption in place unless the property is transferred, the person no longer lives there, or the property use changes; for surviving spouses, remarriage also ends the exemption.

SD-2026-HB1194.s: This law lets the Cosmetology Commission count relevant work experience toward some education hours for certain out-of-state licensure applicants. It covers cosmetology, nail technology, and esthetics licenses, and also applies to some cosmetology-related licenses that are not equivalent in this state. The commission must also adopt rules on this process.

SD-2026-HB1197.s: This law changes where adoption petitions may be filed in circuit court in South Dakota. A petition may be filed in the county where the adopting parent lives, where the agency caring for the child is located, or where the child was born or lives.

SD-2026-HB1201.s: This act became law and lets booster clubs conduct bingo games, lotteries, and use pull-tab devices under state rules. It also allows certain coin- or bill-operated mechanical pull-tab devices to be sold or furnished to booster clubs and used in some licensed establishments. The act limits who can use these devices, how many may be placed, and who keeps the proceeds.

SD-2026-HB1202.s: This bill would authorize construction of a trades center on the campus of Lake Area Technical College. It would set aside money from the general fund for the South Dakota Board of Technical Education to contract for the project, including classrooms, training labs, student services, and related utilities and services. The money would depend on Lake Area Technical College getting matching funds from gifts, grants, donations, or other sources, and no bonds could be used for the project.

SD-2026-HB1204.s: This bill would create a South Dakota school construction loan fund run by the Department of Education. The fund could make zero-interest loans to school districts to construct or expand a school building, with loan terms set over 20 years and no collateral required. It sets rules for which districts can get loans, how the money would be divided among districts, and what information districts must provide when applying. The state treasurer would transfer money from the general fund to the new fund.

SD-2026-HB1209.s: This bill would require employers with more than fifty employees to verify a new worker’s employment eligibility through the federal e-verify program within twenty days of the worker’s first day on the job. It would also let the attorney general investigate complaints and seek a civil penalty of two-thousand dollars for each violation if federal officials confirm an employer knowingly employed an unauthorized person in violation of federal immigration law. The bill would also make it a Class 1 misdemeanor for any individual to knowingly submit false information or documents to evade the e-verify check.

SD-2026-HB1213.s: This bill would set aside $2,500,000 from the general fund for the Department of Education. The money would be used for grants to school districts and accredited nonpublic schools as part of a statewide educator retention initiative. The department could also use up to 5% of the money to administer the grants.

SD-2026-HB1215.s: This law lets counties and municipalities approve licenses for cigar bars in their areas. A cigar bar must meet certain conditions, including having a humidor, enclosed walls, a ventilation system, and getting at least 10% of its yearly income from cigar sales. Licensed cigar bars may allow smoking cigars bought on the premises, but not other tobacco products, and the local government can suspend or revoke a license for certain violations.

SD-2026-HB1219.s: This law requires state agencies to provide a disinterested interpreter or translator when a witness or party needs one in an administrative contested case. The agency must pay for reasonable and just services from its own appropriated funds. A prevailing party may also recover some interpreter or translator costs that were necessarily incurred in gathering evidence or bringing the case.

SD-2026-HB1220.s: This law sets rules for the sale and shipment of nicotine products in South Dakota. It requires most sellers and distributors to have a license, keep records, and follow age-check and delivery rules for certain shipments to consumers. It also creates penalties for selling or shipping nicotine products in violation of the law and puts license fees into a nicotine enforcement fund.

SD-2026-HB1225.s: This bill would direct the Legislature to enhance the future of education in South Dakota. It applies to education in South Dakota, but it does not say how that would be done.

SD-2026-HB1227.s: This law requires owners of electric motor vehicles to pay an annual fee at the time of annual registration. The fee does not apply to an electric motorcycle if the license fee is paid under another section. The money from this fee goes to the state highway fund.

SD-2026-HB1230.s: This bill would change how employers pay the employer's investment in South Dakota's future fee. It would require the department to create a form for employers to opt in or opt out, publish it online, and send paper copies each quarter until the employer responds. Employers that opt out would not have to pay the fee or face penalties for not paying it.

SD-2026-HB1232.s: This law tells state agencies to consult with tribal governments when they make or run programs that could affect tribal members on a reservation. It lists guiding principles such as cooperation, respect for tribal sovereignty, early communication, accountability, and preserving the tribal-state relationship. It also says the section does not create any substantive rights for any party.

SD-2026-HB1233.s: This law changes when the state department may enter into tax collection agreements with an Indian tribe. The agreements can cover listed state taxes and matching tribal taxes, and they may let the department keep an agreed-upon share of gross revenue as an administrative fee.

SD-2026-HB1234.s: This act changes how subpoenas are handled in contested cases under state administrative law. Before a subpoena for documents is served, notice and a copy of the subpoena must be served on each party to the case. A hearing examiner or administrative law judge may quash or modify the subpoena if it is unreasonable and oppressive, or require the person asking for it to pay the reasonable cost of producing the records.

SD-2026-HB1238.s: This law lets financial institutions delay or refuse certain transactions for a consenting, senior, or vulnerable adult if they reasonably believe financial exploitation may have occurred, may be attempted, is occurring, or is being attempted. It also lets them stop account changes, fund transfers, and some beneficiary changes, and it allows them to notify certain third parties in some cases. The law gives financial institutions and their employees immunity from civil, criminal, or administrative liability for actions taken under it.

SD-2026-HB1241.s: This bill would change the notice rules before a school district or other taxing district votes to impose an excess tax levy. It would require public notice at least twenty-one days before the vote and would list the maximum amount, the amount allowed without the levy, the hearing details, the estimated property tax increase, and the intended use of the money. For school districts, it would also change how voters can refer an excess tax levy to a vote and require the ballot to show the number of years the levy applies and the total maximum dollar amount of taxes payable.

SD-2026-HB1244.s: This law repeals the special donations fund and transfers any money in that fund to the general fund. It gives $500,000 from the general fund to the Department of Education for a grant to a nonprofit in the state. The grant is for school districts and accredited nonpublic schools that implement the Jobs for America's Graduates program, and it may be used only for matching private donations, matching certain federal grants, or supporting collaborative efforts.

SD-2026-HB1245.s: This law lets municipalities create a local funding mechanism for capital improvement projects. It allows a municipality to set up a capital improvement board, ask voters to approve a gross receipts tax, and put the money into a special capital outlay fund. The fund may be used only to buy or lease property or equipment, or to build, repair, or renovate real property owned by the municipality, and the law was signed by the Governor.

SD-2026-HB1249.s: This law changes the School Finance Accountability Board and how its recommendations are approved. The board can review school district finances, reduce state aid, impose penalties, or waive some reductions or penalties if a district shows special circumstances. It also lets the board set rules for waiver requests and consider the impact of employee retirements.

SD-2026-HB1250.s: This law revises which community-based providers are covered for state funded services. It applies to services paid with federal funding, Medicaid, block grant funds, state general funds, and other funds from the Department of Social Services or the Department of Human Services. The covered providers include nursing facilities, assisted living facilities, in-home service providers, group care providers, psychiatric residential treatment facilities, substance abuse disorder treatment and prevention providers, community mental health centers, and other listed provider types.

SD-2026-HB1251.s: This act creates two state funds: one for target teacher salary supplements and one for community-based providers. The Department of Education would administer the teacher fund, and the Department of Human Services would administer the community-based providers fund. It also changes how certain unobligated cash balances are moved, including transfers to these two funds and to the general revenue placement fund.

SD-2026-HB1253.s: This bill would change how owner-occupied single-family dwellings and nonagricultural property are assessed for property taxes. Starting with the 2027 assessment year, the assessed value would be the lesser of fair market value or the prior year’s assessed value plus 5 percent, with a full fair market value assessment every fifth assessment year. The changes would not apply to value from new construction, reconstruction, improvements, or additions for the first assessment after that work, or to property assessed under chapters 10-28 to 10-38.

SD-2026-HB1254.s: This act exempts certain soil amendments from sales tax when they are used exclusively for agricultural purposes. It applies to sales of soil amendment products as defined in state law.

SD-2026-HB1258.s: This act requires property tax bills sent to taxpayers to include a QR code and an internet address. These must link to a Department of Revenue website with more information on property taxes and property tax relief programs in South Dakota. The bill also requires the tax bill to tell taxpayers they can find more tax information by using the QR code and internet address.

SD-2026-HB1259.s: This bill would require the Department of Revenue to maintain a public website where property owners can submit applications and documentary evidence for certain property tax relief programs. It also lets applicants use the website for several existing property tax relief applications, including programs for veterans, surviving spouses, tax assessment freezes, tax reductions, and refunds. County treasurers would still help applicants who ask for assistance and receive online applications from the department.

SD-2026-HB1260.s: This act lets a municipality pass an ordinance to create a property tax rebate program. The rebate may go to an owner of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling in the municipality, and only municipal property taxes may be rebated.

SD-2026-HB1261.s: This act would create a property tax credit for owner-occupied single-family dwellings. For property taxes payable in 2027, a county treasurer would apply the credit to each tax bill sent to the owner, and the credit would be the lesser of five hundred dollars or the amount of property tax imposed in 2027. It would also transfer $101 from the South Dakota housing infrastructure fund to the general fund and appropriate $202 to the Department of Revenue.

SD-2026-HB1262.s: This act makes an appropriation from the general fund to the Department of Education for a grant to an eligible nonprofit organization. The grant is for acquiring, renovating, and equipping a facility in Brown County that may offer non-residential, school-based, therapeutic services for students in an alternative setting. The nonprofit may not use the money for residential treatment, inpatient services, or twenty-four-hour care for a student.

SD-2026-HB1263.s: This act changes the definition of an agricultural equipment dealer in South Dakota law. It says a dealer is a person whose sales of the manufacturer’s equipment are equal to or more than thirty percent of the dealer’s gross agricultural equipment sales during the previous calendar year.

SD-2026-HB1264.s: This law eliminates the Agricultural Land Assessment Implementation and Oversight Advisory Task Force. It lets the Department of Revenue receive recommendations from an entity that contracts with the department on agricultural land value. The department must also provide a report to the Taxation Committees on the data it compiles for agricultural value.

SD-2026-HB1265.s: This law allows egg salvage activity for certain bird eggs if a person has a migratory bird special purpose salvage permit from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. It does not allow salvage of eggs from birds whose taking or killing is prohibited at all times, and it keeps the ban on taking, possessing, breaking, or destroying protected nests and eggs in other cases.

SD-2026-HB1270.s: This bill would create a legal apprenticeship path to become a licensed attorney in South Dakota. It would be open to graduates of the University of South Dakota School of Law who are South Dakota residents and who complete supervised apprenticeship work with a qualified attorney. It also requires a criminal background check before licensure and requires newly licensed attorneys to do pro bono legal services for five years.

SD-2026-HB1274.s: This law prohibits knowingly dispensing, distributing, selling, or advertising certain articles or things for use in an unlawful abortion. It also keeps the existing felony penalty for abortion-related conduct under state law. The attorney general may seek a civil penalty, attorney fees, costs, and an injunction against a person who violates the law.

SD-2026-HB1275.s: This bill creates rules for application stores in South Dakota. It requires them to ask for a user’s age category and verify it, and if the user is a minor, the account must be linked to a parent account. The store must get verifiable parental consent before a minor can download, install, or buy an app, or make an in-app purchase. It also sets disclosure rules for parents and adds penalties for violations.

SD-2026-HB1278.s: This bill would stop certain political committees tied to a state official from accepting contributions from some state employees who work for that official. It applies to employees who head a department or agency, are the highest paid employee below the head, or report directly to the official. It defines “state official” to include the Governor, lieutenant governor, certain statewide officers, a Public Utilities Commission commissioner, and members of the Legislature.

SD-2026-HB1279.s: This bill would let technical college employees join the state health plan. A technical college could join the plan on terms agreed to by the human resources commissioner and the college president. Technical college employees who take part would be treated as plan-eligible employees, and the college would make contributions and handle payroll deductions in place of the state. The act would take effect on July 1, 2027.

SD-2026-HB1280.s: This law makes it a Class 6 felony to operate a drone over a prison, correctional facility, jail, juvenile detention facility, or military facility unless the administrator allows it. It also lets law enforcement use approved mitigation techniques and countermeasures in response to a violation. The Department of Public Safety may set rules for those techniques and for training officers on how to use them.

SD-2026-HB1292.s: This act limits when a health carrier may recoup, recover, or retroactively deny a previously paid claim. In most cases, the carrier may do this only within eighteen months after payment and only if it gives the provider written notice of the reason. The limit does not apply in several listed cases, including fraud, waste or abuse, certain other coverage arrangements, and claims for services already paid for, and the Division of Insurance may enforce the law.

SD-2026-HB1293.s: This bill would appropriate $6.8 million from the general fund to the Department of Social Services to increase benefit amounts for the temporary assistance for needy families program. It would set those benefit amounts at the same level as fiscal year 2025 until July 1, 2027. The bill also declares an emergency and would take effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-HB1298.s: This law prohibits publishing a judicial officer’s or law enforcement officer’s home address, date of birth, or social security number by electronic means without the officer’s consent, if it is done with the intent to place the officer or the officer’s immediate family in reasonable fear of death or great bodily injury. A violation is a Class 6 felony and applies to people who publish that information.

SD-2026-HB1299.s: This act lets certain lodging establishments apply for a permit to use a biological filtration system in a water recreational facility. It applies only to lodging establishments with fifteen or fewer sleeping rooms, and only if they get a permit from the department. The permit lasts one year, and the department must inspect the system every year and revoke the permit if the establishment fails an inspection.

SD-2026-HB1300.s: This act exempts some applicants who are victims of human trafficking or domestic abuse from certain clemency notice requirements. To qualify, the person must give the Board of Pardons and Paroles an affidavit and affidavits from two professionals saying the person is a victim and that the person’s safety is at risk if personal information is published in a newspaper. It does not waive any other victim notification rights under state law.

SD-2026-HB1302.s: This bill says the Legislature shall address issues facing South Dakota. It does not give any further details about what issues would be addressed or how.

SD-2026-HB1308.s: This bill would reduce certain property taxes on owner-occupied single-family homes. It would also raise certain gross receipts taxes and use taxes on many sales and services, including retail sales, utilities, telecommunications, rentals, passenger transportation, and amusement devices. The tax changes would affect businesses that collect these taxes and people who buy the taxed goods and services.

SD-2026-HB1311.s: This act requires the South Dakota Board of Technical Education and the Board of Regents to report funding they receive from a foreign source. The annual report must list the amount, source, type, purpose, ongoing relationship, and certain documents for each instance of funding. The report must be posted on each board’s website each year, and the rules apply only to funding received on or after July 1, 2026.

SD-2026-HB1313.s: This act requires South Dakota schools to use resources recommended by the Board of Education Standards for age-appropriate, research-based instruction in prenatal human growth and development. The instruction must include a high-definition ultrasound video or computer-generated rendering that shows prenatal development from fertilization through birth and lasts at least three minutes. It also bars certain materials from entities that perform abortions, promote abortion, or are affiliated with or refer to such entities.

SD-2026-HB1320.s: This act changes who can receive written notice for an appeal of a county board decision. A person appealing can serve notice on a county auditor, a county commissioner, the county state's attorney, or a person the board names to accept notice. If the state's attorney brings the appeal, notice must be served on the person or people affected by the board's decision.

SD-2026-HB1322.s: This bill would change the rules for what a correctional facility must provide when an inmate is discharged, including suitable clothing, a sum of money set by the secretary of corrections, and transportation. The inmate could choose transportation to the county where they lived when the offense happened, the county where they were sentenced, or a location that is the same distance from those two counties, whichever is less.

SD-2026-HB1323.s: This bill would change the rules for referring county and municipal ordinances and resolutions to voters. It would let registered voters file a petition within twenty days after publication, with signatures from at least five percent of registered voters or two thousand five hundred voters, whichever is fewer, and it would keep some measures from being referred. It also changes the notice and referendum rules for school district excess tax levies and related opt out decisions.

SD-2026-HB1326.s: This act sets state spending for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. It appropriates money for the legislative, judicial, and executive departments, state institutions, interest on the public debt, and common schools. It also makes budget changes for several state offices and agencies, including the governor’s office, finance and management, human resources and administration, and information and technology.

SD-2026-HCHC8013.s: This commemoration recognizes the Agricultural Issues team of the West Central FFA chapter in Hartford, South Dakota. It says the team researched and discussed the agricultural, environmental, and economic pros and cons of new autonomous systems in agriculture, and presented before the House and Senate Agriculture and Natural Resources committees. It also celebrates the chapter for placing first in the 2025 State Leadership Development Events and for its journey to nationals.

SD-2026-HCHC8014.s: This commemoration honors the life and legacy of William Long IV. It says he died while ice fishing on the Rosebud Reservation and describes him as a husband, father, brother, friend, boxer, and assistant coach for the Todd County Lady Falcons basketball team. It also extends sympathy to his wife, child, family members, teammates, players, and friends.

SD-2026-HCHC8015.s: This commemoration honors Alice Simonson of Day County, who is believed to be the oldest living South Dakotan. It says she spent most of her life in Day County and has contributed to her community for more than a century. The measure also notes her marriage, her family, her farm records, her church membership, and her service on the original board that built Sun Dial Manor in Bristol.

SD-2026-HCHC8016.s: This legislative commemoration honors the South Dakota Health Care Association for its seventy-five years of service. It says the group has focused on assistance and long-term care services, and on helping individuals, families, and community leaders learn about planning for long-term care for elderly individuals and persons with disabilities.

SD-2026-HCHC8017.s: This commemoration honors the Harrisburg Tigers gymnastics team as the 2026 Class AA state gymnastics champion. It says the team also won the Eastern South Dakota Conference and Metro Conference meets. The commemoration names individual gymnasts and coaches who helped the team’s success.

SD-2026-HCHC8018.s: This commemoration celebrates the seventy-fifth anniversary of the Legislative Research Council. It recognizes the council and its past and present staff for supporting the South Dakota Legislature with legislative operations, information technology, bill drafting and research, and fiscal analysis.

SD-2026-HCHC8019.s: This commemoration honors Dr. Kelly Glodt for his retirement as superintendent of the Pierre School District. It says he has served since 2007 and plans to retire after the September 8, 2025, school board meeting, with retirement effective June 30, 2026. It also recognizes his leadership, service to the district and community, and his work on education policy and statewide conversations.

SD-2026-HCHC8020.s: This commemoration honors the life of Dale Weber and his work with the South Dakota Amateur Baseball Association. It says he played amateur baseball, served as president of the association for many years, and worked to grow baseball in South Dakota. It also honors his contributions to the game and to his community of Salem.

SD-2026-HCHC8021.s: This commemoration honors the life and service of Yvonne Jane "Tiny D" DeCory of Pine Ridge, South Dakota. It says she devoted her life to Lakota youth and worked with schools, churches, community organizations, and tribal programs to help them through grief, trauma, and other hardships. It also says she shared Lakota language, ceremony, and teachings, and gave her time, home, humor, and strength to others.

SD-2026-HCHC8022.s: This commemoration honors Cecelia Fire Thunder for her achievements, leadership, and lifelong public service. It says she served as the first woman elected president of the Oglala Sioux Tribe and has worked as a nurse, health educator, and community organizer.

SD-2026-HCHC8023.s: This legislative commemoration honors the legacy and strength of grandmothers in South Dakota. It says grandmothers are an example of love, wisdom, resilience, and sacrifice for families and communities. It also recognizes grandmothers in Lakota, Dakota, and Nakota traditions as wisdom keepers, ceremonial leaders, and decision-makers.

SD-2026-HCHC8024.s: This legislative commemoration honors the life and legacy of Elizabeth Cook-Lynn, a citizen of the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe. It says she helped pioneer Native American studies through her writing, scholarship, advocacy, and teaching, and it recognizes her work in Native American studies and Indigenous literature.

SD-2026-HCHC8025.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes Josie Hill of Rapid City for her accomplishments in basketball and her commitment to service in her community and the state. It says she played at Rapid City Central High School, Chicago State University, and the University of South Dakota, where she reached her one thousandth career point and helped the Coyotes to a 22-8 record and third-place finish in the Summit League. It also says she is an enrolled member of the Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate and a role model for Indigenous youth.

SD-2026-HCHC8026.s: This commemoration recognizes the nonprofit Oaye Luta Okolakiciye, also called "Moving Forward in a Sacred Way." The organization works to help and strengthen Lakota communities by working with tribal programs, state agencies, and others to provide trauma-informed care based in Lakota spirituality, language, and kinship systems. It supports families and behavioral health on reservations and in surrounding communities in South Dakota, and it is described as volunteer-driven and focused on peer support, prevention, and long-term healing.

SD-2026-HCHC8027.s: This legislative commemoration honors Barbara Dull Knife and describes her service, generosity, and quiet strength. It says she worked as a child welfare advocate and victim witness advocate, founded an emergency safe house for children on the Pine Ridge Reservation, and served on the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council. It also recognizes her work as a board member, elder knowledge keeper, and cultural teacher.

SD-2026-HCHC8028.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes Marvin Richard III of Pine Ridge for his high school athletic career. It says he played basketball, cross country, football, golf, and track and field for Pine Ridge High School, and notes his football and basketball honors, including an all-state quarterback recognition and a South Dakota boys basketball single-game scoring record. It also says he will play for the University of South Dakota Coyotes this fall.

SD-2026-HCRHCR6015.s: This resolution encourages the Executive Board of the Legislative Research Council to form an interim legislative committee to study county boards of mental illness. The study would look at the boards’ authority, voluntary and involuntary commitment processes, training for board members, and ways the information they send might connect with the national instant criminal background check system. It would also involve the Attorney General, the Unified Judicial System, mental health boards, behavioral health providers, and sheriffs.

SD-2026-HJRHJR5001.s: This measure would ask voters to amend the state constitution at the next general election. It would require a public declaration showing the necessity for taking or damaging private property by eminent domain. It also says public use does not include an increase in the tax base, tax revenues, employment, or general economic health.

SD-2026-SB100.s: This law changes several trust rules in South Dakota. It lets certain trusts reimburse a trustor for personal income tax liability in some cases, sets rules for moving assets from one trust to another, and says some lifetime gifts or trust distributions are not counted as advancements unless written conditions are met. It also limits duties and privilege waivers for attorneys working with fiduciaries and changes deadlines and proof rules for some fraudulent transfer claims involving trusts.

SD-2026-SB101.s: This act changes the rules for South Dakota presidential electors. It requires electors to notify the Governor they are present and ready, and it sets steps for filling vacant elector seats if someone does not appear, resigns, refuses to vote, or tries to vote for someone else. It also requires electors to sign a pledge and says they must vote for the candidates whose slate got the most votes in the state's general election, unless a listed exception applies.

SD-2026-SB102.s: This law changes how gaming tax and other gaming revenues are divided in South Dakota. It sends part of the gaming tax to the tourism promotion fund and Lawrence County, pays commission expenses, and then gives the remaining funds to the state general fund, municipalities in Lawrence County except Deadwood, certain school districts in Lawrence County, and the City of Deadwood. It also moves some money to the historical preservation loan and grant fund.

SD-2026-SB106.s: This law changes how much state aid for special education the Department of Education must set aside for extraordinary expenses. Beginning July 1, 2026, the secretary must set aside five million dollars, and the total reserved each year cannot be more than five million five hundred thousand dollars. It applies to special education programs or services for children with disabilities.

SD-2026-SB107.s: This law expands the definition of a “community safety zone” to include licensed and registered child care programs. It affects people who are required to register as sex offenders, because they may not establish or live in a residence within a community safety zone unless one of the listed exceptions applies.

SD-2026-SB110.s: This bill passed and regulates how broadband internet access service providers use customer personal information. It limits when providers may use, disclose, sell, or allow access to that information, and it requires customer opt-in consent in many cases. It also requires notice to customers, lets customers withdraw consent, and requires providers to use reasonable security measures. The bill also allows certain uses for providing service, billing, legal compliance, emergency services, and marketing with an opt-out.

SD-2026-SB111.s: This act requires some social media companies to give a user a copy of the user's personal data when the user asks for it. It also requires those companies to provide transparent interoperability interfaces so users can share selected personal data and, with permission, let third parties access user-created content and updates. The requirements apply to social media services with more than one hundred million active monthly users whose main focus is not charity or religion, and they do not apply to certain religious organizations.

SD-2026-SB113.s: This law increases the penalty for a person who uses threat or violence to intentionally stop another person from carrying out a lawful act required or recommended by that person’s religion. It applies to anyone who does that in South Dakota and makes the offense a Class 6 felony.

SD-2026-SB114.s: This law makes ballot images and cast vote records from automatic tabulating equipment public records. It says a county auditor does not have to produce them if the equipment used in the county does not create them. It also bars release of certain records if they show when or in what order a ballot was cast, include unredacted personal information, or are tied to small groups of ballots unless they are redacted and combined as required.

SD-2026-SB115.s: This law removes the ban on shooting mourning doves in certain areas covered by state hunting rules. It affects people hunting on highways or other public rights-of-way, including areas within the six hundred sixty-foot safety zone rules that already apply to occupied dwellings, churches, schoolhouses, and livestock.

SD-2026-SB116.s: This act gives the Board of Regents $13,330,000 to design and build an indoor athletics facility at Dakota State University in Madison. The project can include furnishings, equipment, and related work such as utilities, sidewalks, parking, and landscaping. It also declares an emergency, so the act takes effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB117.s: This law appropriates money for the Board of Regents to design and build a new soccer venue at South Dakota State University. It allows the board to contract for planning, site preparation, construction, furnishing, equipment, and related work, and to use donated money and other outside funds for the project. The law also declares an emergency and takes effect when approved.

SD-2026-SB118.s: This bill would require the state treasurer to deposit certain tax revenues into a homeowner tax reduction fund each year. The money would come from taxes collected under several tax chapters, and those revenues would no longer go to the general fund except as provided in this bill. If Senate Bill 125 does not become effective, the treasurer could not make these transfers.

SD-2026-SB119.s: This law creates the capitol restoration fund and puts it under the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration. The fund is for restoring, renovating, and improving the state capitol building, and money can be spent only through a special appropriation by the Legislature. The state treasurer must transfer $1,100,000 from the public buildings fund to the new fund.

SD-2026-SB120.s: The bill would appropriate $101 from the general fund to the state for economic development of South Dakota. It also says the state must approve vouchers, the state auditor must draw warrants to pay authorized expenses, and unused money must revert under state law.

SD-2026-SB121.s: This act transfers money from the trust fund for unclaimed property to the general fund. It then appropriates that money to the Office of the Commissioner of School and Public Lands for replacing the Richmond Lake dam and spillway. It also declares an emergency.

SD-2026-SB125.s: The bill would create a new state fund called the homeowner tax reduction fund. The Department of Revenue would run the fund, and it would be used to provide property tax relief for owner-occupied single-family dwellings. Money in the fund could not be moved to the general fund.

SD-2026-SB129.s: This law updates several South Dakota building code references to the 2024 editions of the International Building Code, International Property Maintenance Code, and International Residential Code. It applies to local rules for building standards, property maintenance, and residential construction. It also says some types of buildings and homes are not covered by these rules, including residential structures, mobile or manufactured homes, and farmsteads in certain sections.

SD-2026-SB130.s: This law makes an $8,000,000 appropriation from the general fund to the South Dakota Ellsworth Development Authority. The money must be used for public roadway and related infrastructure improvements needed because of construction activity at Ellsworth Air Force Base, including road work, traffic safety, engineering, and design. The authority must report on each award, and it may not spend more than 3% of the total appropriation on administrative expenses. The act also declares an emergency and is in force after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB131.s: This law lets a nonprofit organization host a special pheasant hunt for disabled veterans and Purple Heart recipients. The hunt may be held during the private shooting preserve season, and no fee may be charged by the state or the sponsoring organization. The Game, Fish and Parks Commission must make rules to run these hunts.

SD-2026-SB132.s: This law changes rules for the South Dakota Veterans Council. It requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to consult with the council twice a year on matters related to veterans and their dependents. The council gives recommendations on budgets, legislation, policies, and programs that affect veterans and their dependents in the state.

SD-2026-SB133.s: The law adds more legislative oversight over state agency rulemaking. It requires agencies to prepare a regulatory impact analysis for proposed permanent rules, including costs, benefits, alternatives, and effects on small business. It also gives the Interim Rules Review Committee more options for major rules, including sending a rule back for changes, declaring the process complete, or recommending that the rule be brought as legislation. For some permanent major rules, the rulemaking is not complete unless statute specifically directs its adoption, amendment, or repeal.

SD-2026-SB134.s: This law changes how state courts and hearing officers interpret state statutes, administrative rules, and policies. It says they may consider a state agency's interpretation, but may not defer to it and must decide the meaning de novo. In cases brought by or against state agencies, any remaining doubt must be resolved in favor of a reasonable interpretation that fits an individual's fundamental constitutional rights.

SD-2026-SB135.s: This law sets rules for data centers in South Dakota. Electric providers must use separate terms for data centers and make them pay costs fairly tied to their service demand and utility use. Local governments keep the authority to limit or regulate data centers, and data center operators must give water-use notices, reports, and public information about their water use.

SD-2026-SB136.s: This act makes a $5,000,000 appropriation from the general fund to the Department of Public Safety. The money is for grants to help volunteer fire departments buy personal protective equipment for firefighters, and the department must give priority to departments with the greatest need.

SD-2026-SB137.s: This law sets up procedures for anti-SLAPP cases involving claims based on a person’s protected public expression. It lets a party ask the court to dismiss part or all of a claim and pauses most other proceedings while that motion is considered. The law also sets deadlines for hearings and rulings, and it allows court costs, attorney fees, and litigation expenses to be awarded in some cases.

SD-2026-SB138.s: This act changes when a recount for a school board election must be finished. A candidate who loses by no more than 2 percent may ask for a recount within 5 days after the official canvass. The recount must be completed before the annual meeting of the school board.

SD-2026-SB139.s: This law revises what a correctional facility official must provide when an inmate is discharged. It requires suitable clothing, a sum of money set by the secretary of corrections, and transportation to certain counties or a similar location. It applies to inmates leaving a correctional facility by parole, suspended sentence, or final discharge.

SD-2026-SB14.s: This law changes South Dakota rules for pharmacies and the Board of Pharmacy. It updates definitions, licensing, renewal, ownership changes, pharmacist-in-charge rules, and the board’s rulemaking powers. It also allows licensed pharmacies to use remote drop sites to deliver prescription drugs to patients under a pharmacist’s supervision, and it changes how pharmacies handle delivery outside the pharmacy.

SD-2026-SB142.s: This law changes when certain political committees must file campaign finance disclosure statements with the secretary of state. It covers candidates and campaign committees for statewide, legislative, and county offices, as well as statewide political action committees, political parties, county political parties and auxiliary organizations, and statewide ballot question committees. It also allows termination statements in certain cases and sets penalties for violations.

SD-2026-SB15.s: This law creates the Developmental Disability Service Delivery Committee. The committee will review Medicaid waiver programs for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, hear from the Department of Human Services, and seek feedback from individuals, family members, providers, and case management organizations. It will also consider changes to improve services and efficiency and report its work and recommendations each year. The act expires on January 1, 2030.

SD-2026-SB154.s: This law changes the rules for classifying some homes as owner-occupied for tax purposes. It says an owner-occupied single-family dwelling includes garages and other related structures on the same land. It also says a person may have only one principal residence classified this way, and a contractor may have up to four dwellings classified this way under certain rules.

SD-2026-SB156.s:
This law changes South Dakota’s animal cruelty crime. If a person commits that offense in an especially depraved, heinous, sadistic, or wicked way, it becomes a Class 4 felony.

It affects people who commit the cruelty-to-an-animal offense under state law.

SD-2026-SB164.s: This act requires a person to show proficiency in English before being issued a commercial driver license in South Dakota. It also allows the department to set rules for checking English proficiency, including giving knowledge and skills tests in English. If a driver is cited for a traffic offense or is in a traffic accident, law enforcement must check English proficiency, and a driver who does not meet the requirement can be cited and placed out of service. The act creates misdemeanor penalties for operating a commercial motor vehicle without sufficient English language proficiency.

SD-2026-SB165.s: This act revises several rules for municipal government in South Dakota. It changes how mayor vacancies are filled, when appointed and elected municipal officers begin serving, and who may be removed from office. It also updates rules for municipal finance officers, city attorneys, city engineers, law enforcement officers, and civil service systems.

SD-2026-SB171.s: This law changes how absentee ballots are received, processed, and counted in South Dakota. It allows the person in charge of the election to create an absentee ballot precinct and sets rules for poll watchers to observe the process. It also repeals one section of current law and takes effect as an emergency measure when signed.

SD-2026-SB172.s: This bill says the Legislature shall enhance the economy of South Dakota. It does not give any other details about how that would be done.

SD-2026-SB174.s: This bill would appropriate $5,000,000 from the general fund to the Department of Education. The money would be granted directly to school districts to help cover operational costs. Each district would receive a pro rata share based on its 2026 fall enrollment compared with statewide enrollment.

SD-2026-SB175.s: This law requires a person to show proof of United States citizenship when registering to vote. It lists several documents that can be used, including certain state or tribal ID cards, a birth certificate, a passport, or a naturalization certificate. It also changes rules for some voters who do not provide citizenship documentation or who use only a mail box address, and it was signed by the Governor.

SD-2026-SB176.s: This act changes when voted ballots, pollbooks, and other election materials may be destroyed after an election. It lets officials destroy them twenty-two months after municipal, nonfederal, federal, and school district elections. For federal elections, if a ballot is used for both federal and state or local races, the ballots and other election material must be kept for twenty-two months.

SD-2026-SB177.s: This law changes how optical scan ballots are marked in South Dakota. Election officials must provide a black ink pen for each in-person voter and tell absentee voters to use a black ink pen. Officials may not disqualify a ballot just because it was marked with a writing instrument other than a black ink pen.

SD-2026-SB179.s: This law lets a court commit a juvenile who has been adjudicated delinquent to the Department of Corrections only if the judge finds no viable alternative and that it is the least restrictive option. It applies to juveniles adjudicated delinquent for certain offenses, including some weapons offenses, as well as other listed serious offenses. The court must put its findings in the written decree.

SD-2026-SB180.s: This act changes the rules for nondomiciled commercial learner’s permits and commercial driver licenses in South Dakota. It limits who may apply, including certain noncitizens with H-2A, H-2B, or E-2 visas and people domiciled in a U.S. territory with those visas.
