It also requires certain documents and checks, sets the license expiration rules, and says the department may downgrade a license if the holder is no longer eligible.

SD-2026-SB183.s: This law changes the notice rules before a school district or other taxing district votes on an excess tax levy. At least twenty-one days before the vote, the district must publish notice in a legal newspaper and on its website, and send it to all property owners. The notice must list the amount under consideration, the amount allowed without an excess tax levy, the hearing date, time, and location, the estimated property tax increase, and how the money will be used. Taxpayers must also be given a chance to comment at the public hearing.

SD-2026-SB193.s: This bill changes the definition of "backup electric generation" to mean electric generation that is not connected to the grid and is used on a temporary basis when the main power source is unavailable. It also says backup electric generation is not an "energy conversion facility" under this chapter. The change would affect electric generation facilities and the permitting rules in this law.

SD-2026-SB196.s: This bill would raise the household income limits for a real property tax assessment freeze on an owner-occupied single-family dwelling. It would apply to individuals who meet the other requirements in the chapter, including the residency and dwelling-use rules, and to a surviving spouse who meets those conditions. The income limits would also increase each year by the index factor starting on the date in the bill.

SD-2026-SB197.s: This law changes how the South Dakota-Ireland Trade Commission is run and how its trade fund is handled. It keeps the commission made up of legislators, state officials, and private-sector representatives, and says the Executive Board of the Legislative Research Council will provide administrative services and administer the fund. The fund is for the commission’s administrative expenses and work, and it includes money raised for the commission plus gifts, grants, and other donations.

SD-2026-SB198.s: This bill would generally bar students from using cell phones during the school day. It would allow cell phone use for approved medical or educational accommodations and during emergencies affecting a student or staff member’s health, safety, or well-being. Each school district board would have to adopt a policy for student discipline if the rule is not followed.

SD-2026-SB199.s: This bill would create a property tax relief fund in the state treasury. The Department of Revenue would administer the fund, and money in it would be used to help pay property tax levies of local political subdivisions. The goal is to reduce property taxes on real property. The state treasurer would transfer money from the general fund into the new fund based on increases in general fund money.

SD-2026-SB204.s: This law revises the rules for loans from the South Dakota housing infrastructure fund. It defines housing infrastructure and public infrastructure for single-family or multi-family housing projects. The authority may make loans for these projects, and the loan principal may not be more than half of the total project cost.

SD-2026-SB205.s: This bill would change the original registration tax for drones based on the purchase price. It would set a lower rate for drones used exclusively for agricultural purposes and a different rate for all other drones, while small unmanned aircraft would not be covered by this section. The bill would also create a drone aviation fund to support training in drone aviation through the technical colleges in the state.

SD-2026-SB206.s: This bill would set aside $100,000 from the general fund for the Legislative Research Council to hire a contractor for a study. The study would look at state and federal laws, regulations, and services for a length of service award program for volunteer firefighters and emergency medical services personnel, and the contractor would report recommendations for implementing such a program.

SD-2026-SB208.s: This bill would change South Dakota law on property classification and assessment appeals. If an owner or taxpayer wins certain appeals, the court would have to award disbursements and reasonable attorney fees, and in some cases it could do so when the reduction is less than 20 percent. It would also let the county receive disbursements and attorney fees when the owner or taxpayer does not prevail, and it would bar these awards if the wrong assessment was caused by the owner or taxpayer hindering the director of equalization.

SD-2026-SB21.s: This act modifies tax refunds for elderly persons and persons with a disability in South Dakota. It changes rules for retail sales and service tax refunds, property tax reductions, and special assessments on owner-occupied single-family dwellings for certain older, disabled, and low-income households. It also repeals several sections of state law.

SD-2026-SB210.s: This bill changes how some wind farm tax revenue is handled for school districts. For wind farms that begin producing power after June 30, 2016, the bill keeps all of that revenue with the school district for the first five years, then phases the amount down over the next four years. It also lets school districts transfer wind energy tax revenue from the general fund to certain other school funds if they meet required state education compliance checks.

SD-2026-SB211.s: This bill would prohibit ambulance service providers from billing or trying to collect from a patient for out-of-network emergency medical services, except for any coinsurance, copayment, or deductible under the patient’s health benefit plan. It would require health benefit plans to reimburse out-of-network ambulance service providers at a set rate, based on the local rate if one exists or, if not, the provider’s billed charge or two hundred seventy-five percent of the medicare allowable rate. It would also require both the ambulance service provider and the health benefit plan to give the patient a clear explanation of benefits and any amount the patient owes.

SD-2026-SB213.s: This bill would create a state program and fund to give grants for out-of-school time programming for students. It would let the Department of Education administer the fund, set grant rules, and spend part of the money on grant administration. It would also change certain filing and reporting fees and direct money from those fees and from the general fund into the new fund.

SD-2026-SB214.s: This law requires the secretary of state to post the complete statewide voter registration file on the secretary's website each week and to keep a rolling five-year historical archive of that file online. The archive must be free to use, and certain personal information, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, nondriver ID numbers, and month and day of birth, is not open to public inspection. The law also says information from the statewide or county voter registration files may not be sold or used for a commercial purpose, and it may not be placed on the internet for unrestricted access except as allowed by law.

SD-2026-SB215.s: This bill would create a pilot program for a secured cryptographically end-to-end verifiable voting system in up to three election jurisdictions. It would be used for absentee voters and voters under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and it would let some election laws be waived for the pilot. The bill also sets rules for how the system must work, including voter verification, ballot encryption, auditing, and reporting to state officials. The bill was withdrawn at the request of the prime sponsor.

SD-2026-SB216.s: This bill limits how much the assessed value of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling may increase each year, generally to no more than 3 percent. If the home changes owners, it must be reassessed at fair market value, and additions, expansions, or changes in use can raise the base amount further. The bill also allows taxing districts, in some cases, to use a mill rate above another legal limit if real property tax revenue stays within set growth limits.

SD-2026-SB217.s: This bill would set aside $750,000 from the general fund for a fire management officer position in the Department of Public Safety. The position would support Division of Wildland Fire operations east of the Missouri River. The money not lawfully spent or obligated would revert under state law.

SD-2026-SB219.s: This act requires a state agency to consult the Aeronautics Commission before buying, transferring, or disposing of a state owned and operated aircraft. The commission must give advice and expertise in a written report to the Governor and the agency. The rule does not apply to unmanned aircraft, small unmanned aircraft, or certain aircraft used for educational purposes by the Board of Regents or the South Dakota Board of Technical Education.

SD-2026-SB220.s: This bill would require the Department of Corrections to study juvenile correctional and residential facilities outside South Dakota. The study would look at best practices, therapeutic pod housing models, vocational training, mental health integration, staff-to-youth ratios, and safety protocols. It would also require on-site inspections and interviews at at least three such facilities and a written report to the Legislative Research Council.

SD-2026-SB221.s: This law sets rules for the retail sale of nicotine products in South Dakota and creates a licensing system for retailers and vending machine retailers. It limits who may get a license, requires age checks for vending machine sales, and bars sales to people under 21, free samples, and several types of remote sales. It also requires records to be kept and gives the Department of Revenue authority to inspect, investigate, fine, suspend, or revoke licenses for violations.

SD-2026-SB224.s: This act changes custody law for disputes between parents. If either parent asks for it, there is a rebuttable presumption that joint physical custody is in the minor child’s best interest, unless evidence shows otherwise. It defines joint physical custody as time with the child that is about equal for each parent. The court must still consider the child’s best interests and make written findings unless the parties waive that or reach an agreement.

SD-2026-SB225.s: This bill changes how interest earnings from the unclaimed property trust fund are handled. It sends a distribution amount from that fund to the commissioner of school and public lands for apportionment to school districts. The bill also changes how the trust fund is managed and how the distribution amount is calculated.

SD-2026-SB227.s: This bill would stop an insurer from declaring a motor vehicle a total loss after damage from a collision, fire, vandalism, weather, or another peril unless repair costs are at least seventy-five percent of the vehicle’s actual cash value before the damage. It would still allow a total loss declaration if the vehicle owner asks for it in writing, and it defines actual cash value as the current market value within a radius of two-hundred miles from the owner’s primary address, based on the vehicle’s year, make, model, accessories, options, wear, odometer reading, and accident history.

SD-2026-SB228.s: This law changes several rules for tax increment financing districts in South Dakota. It says county tax formulas for new structures may not be used for property within a tax increment finance district, and it changes how school district tax levies are raised for these districts. It also changes how districts are created, including adding a rule that a county may not create a district inside a municipality without the municipality’s consent.

SD-2026-SB229.s: This bill would require voter approval for some school district capital outlay certificates, lease-purchase contracts, and installment purchase contracts. It applies when the district would owe future payments above certain limits or when the certificates have a maturity date in excess of ten years. It also says approval requires an affirmative vote of at least sixty percent of those voting on the question.

SD-2026-SB230.s: This bill would make an exception for improvement districts from a limit on how much property tax revenue a taxing district may collect each year. It would let those districts be treated differently under the revenue growth limit for property taxes.

SD-2026-SB231.s: This act creates the water infrastructure development fund for rural water projects in South Dakota. The fund may be used for the construction, planning, and development of rural water projects, and the Board of Water and Natural Resources may award grants and loans from it under set limits. The state treasurer must transfer money from the general fund to the new fund, and the act took effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB236.s: This act creates a county and township infrastructure fund in the state treasury. Counties must transfer certain unspent, unobligated rural access infrastructure money to the state treasurer every third year starting in 2029. The Department of Revenue will administer the fund, and spending from it must be budgeted through the general appropriation bill.

SD-2026-SB239.s: This bill would change the reinvestment payment program for certain new or expanded facilities and equipment upgrades. It would set new rules for applying, review, and approval, and it would let some projects use a combined reinvestment payment and direct payment permit. It also would let the Board of Economic Development set the minimum project cost for projects covered by these changes.

SD-2026-SB240.s: This act appropriates $5,000,000 from the general fund to the Department of Revenue for county rural access infrastructure. The money will be deposited into rural access infrastructure funds and distributed to counties based on the number of small structures on township roads and county secondary roads. Counties that receive the money must use it under the rules in state law.

SD-2026-SB243.s: This bill was passed. It imposes a tax on retail transactions and puts the money into a property tax replacement fund. The fund is used to reduce property tax levies on owner-occupied single-family dwellings, agricultural property, and nonagricultural property, and counties must adjust property taxes for the upcoming tax year. It also sets filing rules and penalties for failing to pay the tax or filing a false return.

SD-2026-SB244.s: This measure says the Legislature shall address issues facing South Dakota. It does not name any specific issue, program, or policy change.

SD-2026-SB245.s: This law creates the homeowner property tax reduction fund in the state treasury and puts the Department of Revenue in charge of it. The fund is meant to provide property tax relief for owner-occupied single-family dwellings and to reduce the local effort for general education levies on those homes. It also directs certain tax money into the fund starting on the dates listed in the act and requires a transfer from the general revenue replacement fund to the new fund.

SD-2026-SB25.s: This law updates the permit process for proposed energy conversion and AC/DC conversion facilities in South Dakota. In some counties, the applicant must give written notice to adjacent property owners before filing a permit application, and after filing, it must post public notice signs at the proposed site. It also changes how a local review committee is formed and what it reviews, and it repeals one section of state law.

SD-2026-SB26.s: This law changes state procurement rules so they do not apply to highway construction contracts entered into by the Department of Transportation. It also exempts a political subdivision’s utility contract when it is bid together with a Department of Transportation highway construction contract.

SD-2026-SB27.s: This act revises the description of certain highways in the state trunk highway system. It changes the listed highway routes in several South Dakota counties, including routes near the Wyoming, Nebraska, and Minnesota state lines. It affects the state highway system and the counties named in the act.

SD-2026-SB3.s: This law limits when counties, municipalities, and townships may require a building permit for certain repairs or like-for-like replacements on detached single-family owner-occupied homes. It covers doors, downspouts, fascia, fencing panels or posts, gutters, nonstructural siding, soffit, and windows if the dimensions stay the same. It also says homeowners must still follow other applicable building codes or ordinances, and permits may still be required for designated historical property.

SD-2026-SB30.s: This law changes the reasons someone can use to challenge another registered voter’s eligibility. A challenge may only ask whether the voter has voted or registered in another state, is a resident of South Dakota, or is a United States citizen. The challenge may be filed by the secretary of state, the county auditor where the voter is registered, or another registered voter in the same county.

SD-2026-SB31.s: This law lets county auditors use a confirmation letter or postcard to verify a voter’s registration when a notice comes back as undeliverable. If the voter does not return the confirmation by the deadline, or if the mailing is returned as undeliverable, the voter’s registration must be moved to inactive. The same rules also apply to address verification requests sent under another section of state law.

SD-2026-SB32.s: This law changes ballot rules for certain primary elections. It requires county auditors to put precinct committeeman and precinct committeewoman candidates on the official primary ballot, and it says judicial office candidates must be listed without any party designation. It also repeals two sections of law and takes effect immediately because an emergency is declared.

SD-2026-SB34.s: This act changes rules for municipal and school district elections. It updates who may vote, how voter challenges are handled, when election notices must be published, and when absentee ballots must be available. It also sets different rules when a local election is combined with a primary or general election.

SD-2026-SB35.s: This act revises how a person can request a certified copy of a veteran’s certificate of discharge from a county register of deeds. It says the copy must be provided without charge to the veteran and certain other people, including a Veterans Affairs representative, the veteran’s legal representative, a county or tribal veterans service officer, an accredited veterans service organization representative, or the veteran’s next of kin if the veteran is deceased. A requester must submit a Department of Veterans Affairs form showing they are eligible to get the copy.

SD-2026-SB36.s: This law lets certain utilities create wildfire mitigation plans and submit them for review or filing. The plans must include steps for inspecting and operating equipment, managing vegetation, restoring service after a wildfire, and coordinating with wildfire agencies. Utilities with approved plans may recover certain costs, and the law limits when a person can sue them for wildfire damages.

SD-2026-SB37.s: This act makes state money available for water and environmental projects in South Dakota. It funds grants for studies, flood control planning, water system work, solid waste cleanup, and water quality projects. It also provides money for grants, loans, and technical assistance under state drinking water and water pollution control programs.

SD-2026-SB40.s: This law revises the rules for foreign ownership and leasing of agricultural land in South Dakota. It keeps limits on who may own, lease, or hold an easement on agricultural land, and it allows some exceptions for certain research and livestock feeding leases. It also requires some people to file a copy of their federal foreign land report with the state agriculture department, and it allows the attorney general to enforce the law and collect civil penalties for violations.

SD-2026-SB41.s: This act changes South Dakota law on criminal invasions of privacy. It keeps it illegal to record or share intimate images without consent and adds a ban on creating or sharing digitally fabricated material that makes an identifiable person appear nude or in sexual conduct. It also sets felony and misdemeanor penalties for violations.

SD-2026-SB42.s: This act increases penalties for bringing certain items to inmates in a state correctional facility, including alcoholic beverages, marijuana, cell phones, prescription or nonprescription drugs, controlled substances, dangerous weapons, and other unauthorized articles. It also changes the penalties for knowingly ingesting a controlled drug or substance. The new penalties apply to people in state correctional facilities and, in some cases, to people under parole supervision.

SD-2026-SB43.s: This act changes South Dakota law on search and seizure to include digital currency as "property" under that chapter. It also adds a definition of "digital currency" as a digital representation of value recorded on a secured distributed ledger or other medium of exchange, including blockchain or similar technology.

SD-2026-SB44.s: This law lets the attorney general or a designee seek a subpoena, with judicial approval, for business records in certain criminal investigations involving internet crimes against children or human trafficking. It allows judges in Hughes County to review and issue these subpoenas statewide, and it applies to providers such as internet, electronic communication, remote computing, and telecommunications services. The subpoena may require records like subscriber information, account details, phone numbers, device information, email addresses, and internet addresses. Providers must comply, may be barred from notifying the account holder, and the records must be used only for official law enforcement purposes.

SD-2026-SB45.s: This law makes it unlawful to sell, buy, receive, possess, consume, or give products containing delta-8 tetrahydrocannabinol, delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, THC-O acetate, or hexahydrocannabinol to or by people under the age of twenty-one, unless the substance was obtained directly or with a valid prescription or order from a practitioner. It also covers buying these products on behalf of a person under the age of twenty-one, with an exception for a parent or guardian who meets the same prescription or order rule. A violation of the sale rule is a Class 1 misdemeanor, and a violation of the other rules is a Class 2 misdemeanor.

SD-2026-SB49.s: This law sets rules for direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies that collect or use a consumer’s genetic data. It requires plain-language privacy notices, express consent for collection, sharing, retention, research use, and marketing, and it gives consumers ways to access, delete, and revoke consent for their data and biological samples. Service providers under contract with those companies must follow the same confidentiality rules. The attorney general may seek civil penalties for violations, and several kinds of health, research, education, and law enforcement entities are exempt.

SD-2026-SB54.s: This law revises when money can be taken from the South Dakota deferred compensation plan. It lets a participant who is at least fifty-nine and one-half years old choose an in-service distribution in any form allowed by law. A participant who gets an in-service distribution may still keep making deferrals of compensation into the plan.

SD-2026-SB55.s: This act appropriates $650,000 from the general fund to the extraordinary litigation fund. The money is for payment of eligible expenses under state law, and the commissioner of the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration and the state auditor are responsible for approving and paying the expenditures. It also declares an emergency, so the act is in force after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB60.s: This act restricts certain prohibited entities from holding or controlling real property interests in South Dakota while there is a military installation in the state. It requires some prohibited entities to dispose of covered property interests within a set time and gives the attorney general authority to investigate and enforce the law. The act also lists several exceptions, including some federally approved entities, certain local government-approved transactions, and some individuals with lawful permanent resident, citizen, or lawful status.

SD-2026-SB63.s: This act sets up a state office of apprenticeship within the Department of Labor and Regulation. The office will serve as the state apprenticeship agency, promote registered apprenticeship programs, set standards for those programs, and resolve disputes over apprenticeship agreements. It also requires the department to write rules for registration, oversight, complaints, and reciprocity with programs from other states.

SD-2026-SB67.s: This law appropriates $4,205,497 from the general fund to a special fund for costs related to any emergency or disaster impacting South Dakota. The secretary of the Department of Public Safety must approve vouchers, and the state auditor must draw warrants to pay the authorized expenses.

SD-2026-SB68.s: This law appropriates $2,652,561 from the general fund to the state fire suppression special revenue fund. The money is for costs related to suppressing wildfires impacting the state. It also declares an emergency and says the act takes effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB69.s: This law gives $5,000,000 from the general fund to the Department of Public Safety. The money is for a new Division of Highway Patrol airplane, mission equipment for the airplane, and installing that equipment. It also declares an emergency, so the law takes effect after it is approved.

SD-2026-SB71.s: The Department of Transportation may make an agreement with the federal government to take over some federal environmental review and related duties for highway projects in South Dakota. The state also waives sovereign immunity in federal court for cases involving those duties. If a person wins a case under this law or another highway or public transportation project case tied to it, the state must pay the damages, attorney fees, and costs from the state highway fund.

SD-2026-SB72.s: This act changes the deadline for unspent money appropriated for modernizing the state’s enterprise resource planning systems. Any money from that appropriation that is not lawfully spent or obligated will now revert to the general fund on June 30, 2029.

SD-2026-SB73.s: This law changes several state financial and recordkeeping rules. It requires agencies to file consulting contracts with the state auditor, requires certain contracts to be posted on a searchable state website, and updates rules for record retention and warrant payments. It also changes mileage reimbursement rules for state business and requires electronic submission for certain sealed bids or proposals through an approved procurement system.

SD-2026-SB74.s: This act moves money into the general fund from two state funds. It transfers $80,854,355 from the budget reserve fund and $20,613,269 from the general revenue replacement fund. It also declares an emergency, and the act took effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB75.s: This law changes who can take part in South Dakota’s cybersecurity services initiative. It uses state money to expand and improve cybersecurity for counties, nonprofit drinking water and sanitary sewer utilities, utilities operated by a political subdivision, and municipalities, and it also covers related administrative costs.

SD-2026-SB76.s: This law allows the South Dakota housing infrastructure fund to make loans for airport infrastructure. The loans may go to the owner or operator of an airport with scheduled air service in the state and in a metropolitan statistical area with an estimated annual resident population of at least one hundred twenty-five thousand, and the money must be used to improve or maintain airport infrastructure.

SD-2026-SB78.s: This law revises South Dakota’s fiscal year 2026 state budget. It changes funding for many state offices, departments, and colleges, including general, federal, and other funds. It also changes some full-time equivalent staffing levels for several agencies.

SD-2026-SB79.s: This law makes a $6,000,000 appropriation from the general fund to the South Dakota Board of Technical Education. The money is for building an advanced manufacturing laboratory space and classrooms on the campus of Southeast Technical College. The funding depends on the college receiving $18,000,000 or as much as needed from gifts, grants, donations, or other sources, and on no bonds being issued for the project. The law also declares an emergency, so it takes effect after passage and approval.

SD-2026-SB81.s: This law makes it illegal to maliciously beat, injure, attempt to injure, harass, intimidate, entice, distract, or otherwise interfere with a service animal that is with a person with a disability. It says a service animal is a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, and that emotional support, comfort, or companionship alone do not count. A violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor.

SD-2026-SB82.s: This law makes it illegal for a person to intentionally misrepresent an animal as a service animal in a place of public accommodation to get rights or privileges reserved for a service animal. A violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor. The law defines a service animal as a dog trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability, and says emotional support, comfort, or companionship do not count as those tasks.

SD-2026-SB87.s: This law sets requirements for forensic medical examinations after an alleged rape or sexual offense. It says the county where the offense happened must pay for the exam, including related services, supplies, testing, medication, and radiology. It also says victims do not have to work with law enforcement or join the criminal justice system to get the exam, and it sets rules for consent, provider training, and hospital or clinic policies.

SD-2026-SB88.s: This act sets rules for when a person with authority to take private property for public use may enter land to examine it if the owner does not give permission. It applies only to projects that need a siting permit, and the person must give the owner written notice, have a pending or approved permit application, and pay for any actual damage. The owner may challenge the proposed examination in circuit court, and may ask for a copy of the results.

SD-2026-SB89.s: This law creates a task force to study emergency medical services as an essential service and how to fund it. The task force will look at funding for counties and municipalities, ambulance service payments, and reimbursement for out-of-network emergency medical services. It will also seek input from stakeholders and give the executive board a report with findings and recommendations.

SD-2026-SB90.s: This law expands the information the department must send to the prescription drug monitoring program for each cardholder and nonresident cardholder. The department must send the person’s name, physical address unless the applicant is homeless, date of birth, and registry identification card number.

SD-2026-SB91.s: This law changes the process for asking a county board of commissioners to change a comprehensive plan or zoning ordinances. It says the petition must be filed with the county auditor, who sends it to the commission and the board. The commission must hold a public hearing and make a recommendation, and then the board must hold a public hearing and act on the request.

SD-2026-SB93.s: This bill would change state ethics rules for certain state officers and employees who approve, award, supervise, or administer contracts for a state agency. It would bar them from being employed by an organization that received one of those contracts for one year if the contract was worth $1 million or less, or two years if it was worth more than $1 million. It also keeps limits on taking a direct benefit from certain contracts and allows a governing body to approve some contracts only after written disclosure and review.

SD-2026-SB96.s: This act lets a county impose a gross receipts tax of up to one-half percent on taxable sales, products transferred electronically, and services in the county. The money must go into a county property tax reduction fund and be used to give credits against the county property tax levy on owner-occupied property first, and then on agricultural and nonagricultural property if money remains. The Department of Revenue would administer the tax, and a county would adopt it by ordinance, with voter referral or an initiated ordinance allowed.

SD-2026-SB98.s: This law sets rules for virtual currency kiosks in South Dakota and requires kiosk operators to be licensed. It requires receipts, fraud warnings, customer identity checks, and reports about kiosk activity and complaints. It also sets transaction limits, caps charges, and requires full refunds for certain fraudulent transactions when the user meets the listed conditions.

SD-2026-SCRSCR606.s: This resolution says the Water Management Board should prioritize review and approval of water rights applications and future use reservations from the Missouri River. It applies to South Dakota public water systems and is aimed at meeting future needs of the people of the state. The resolution has passed in the Legislature.

SD-2026-SCRSCR607.s: This resolution supports congressional authorization and federal participation for major rural water supply projects in South Dakota. It says these projects are important for long-term regional water planning and for serving rural water systems, municipalities, regional water suppliers, and South Dakota citizens. It also encourages coordination among local water systems, state agencies, and federal partners.

SD-2026-SCRSCR608.s: This resolution urges community service providers and food service establishments to work together to prevent food waste and reduce hunger in South Dakota. It points to the protections of the 1996 Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act for food donations to nonprofit groups. It affects restaurants, grocery stores, other food service businesses, nonprofits, and people who need food assistance.

SD-2026-SCSC812.s: This legislative commemoration honors Glenn Muller of Davis, South Dakota, and congratulates him on his career and accomplishments. It says he has spent his life in South Dakota's agriculture industry, including work in the pork industry, education, policy advocacy, and public outreach. It also notes awards he received and his role as Executive Director of the South Dakota Pork Producers Council.

SD-2026-SCSC813.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes Solventum’s expansion of its Brookings, South Dakota, manufacturing facility. It says the expansion included an approximately 274,000-square-foot building addition with sixteen new loading docks, and that Solventum will officially open the expanded facility on April 2, 2026.

SD-2026-SCSC814.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes Boys & Girls Clubs in South Dakota for their work with children, teens, and families. It also commends the 2026 Youth of the Year finalists for their accomplishments and successes. The measure notes that youth nominees from clubs in Sioux Falls, Wagner, Mission, Flandreau, and Pierre earned the title of Youth of the Year.

SD-2026-SCSC815.s: This commemoration recognizes Shane Jordan as the 2025 national recipient of the Hugh Hammond Bennett Conservation Planner Award. It says he worked as a district conservationist for Spink and Clark counties and that his work led to more than two hundred fifty conservation stewardship program contracts. The measure also notes that the award honors conservation planning and soil conservation.

SD-2026-SCSC816.s: This commemoration recognizes Generations Indigenous Ways, a Native nonprofit on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. It says the group helps American Indian youth by combining Lakota cultural knowledge with science, technology, engineering, and math education, along with camps, afterschool activities, community science seminars, and food sustainability work. It also says the organization supports families, elders, and cultural traditions in tribal and non-tribal communities.

SD-2026-SCSC817.s: This legislative commemoration honors the Canton C-Hawk girls wrestling team. It says the team won the Region 2 regional tournament for the second year in a row and had 13 wrestlers qualify for the state tournament. It also names two wrestlers who won state championships, Brooke Warejcka and Finley Evjen.

SD-2026-SCSC818.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes and commends Grey Zabel for his athletic achievements with the 2026 Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks. It says he was born and raised in Pierre, graduated from T.F. Riggs High School, and helped teams win state and national championships before being drafted by the Seahawks. The commemoration also says his work ethic and talent have inspired young athletes across South Dakota.

SD-2026-SCSC819.s: This measure honors the Canton C-Hawk girls wrestling team. It says the team won the Region 2 regional tournament for the second straight year and had thirteen wrestlers qualify for the state tournament. It also says two wrestlers won state championships and the team was named the 2026 State Wrestling Tournament champions.

SD-2026-SCSC820.s: This commemoration honors Dr. Margaret Becker as the recipient of the 2025 Copic Humanitarian Award. It says she has provided care at the Monument Health Spearfish Clinic and has served as medical director of the Good Shepherd Free Clinic in Spearfish for the past eight years. It also says she helped people who otherwise would have had to go without medical attention and designated the Good Shepherd Free Clinic to receive the $10,000 Copic donation.

SD-2026-SCSC821.s: This commemoration honors Arthur Mauf for his service to the United States as he approaches his 100th birthday. It says he served aboard the USS General John Pope and in the United States Marine Corps, where he reached the rank of Private First Class. It also says he returned to Madison, South Dakota, where he farmed and built his life there.

SD-2026-SCSC822.s: This commemoration honors TKO’s Custom Catering and Capitol Cafe for its service during the legislative session. It says the team starts work before many legislators arrive and continues providing food throughout the long days in the Capitol Building. The measure recognizes the effect of that service on legislators, staff, and visitors.

SD-2026-SCSC823.s: This legislative commemoration honors Canton C-Hawks wrestling coach Jeremy Ask. It says he was a two-time state champion wrestler at St. Ansgar, Iowa, wrestled for Iowa State University, and coached in Alcester before becoming head coach in Canton in 2001. It also says he coached the girls wrestling program when it was first sanctioned in 2021, became an assistant coach in 2024, and later coached both a girls team and a boys team to state championships in the same year.

SD-2026-SCSC824.s: This commemoration honors the 2025-2026 Canton C-Hawks boys wrestling team. It says the team won the Region 2B tournament and the State B wrestling championship for the ninth year in a row. It also names the state qualifiers and the coaches who led the team.

SD-2026-SCSC825.s: This legislative commemoration honors the life and legacy of Casey Joe Wilson. It says he was a husband, father, member of the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association, a proud member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe, and someone who helped found the South Dakota shared parenting movement.

SD-2026-SCSC826.s: This legislative commemoration honors the Wall High School Eagles as the 2025 Class 9A State Football Champions. It says the team finished a 12-0 season, scored 656 points, and beat the Howard Tigers 60-6 in the championship game. The measure also notes the roles of the coaches, athletic staff, school administrators, and the Wall community.

SD-2026-SCSC827.s: This commemoration honors Ashlan Carlow-Blount for excellence in athletics, academics, and leadership. It says she is an Oglala Lakota tribal member from the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation and a senior at Ma h píya Lúta High School. The resolution describes her achievements in basketball, track and field, cross country, and school, and says she has committed to attend the University of South Dakota.

SD-2026-SCSC828.s: This legislative commemoration honors the life and legacy of Joseph M. Marshall III. It says he was an enrolled member of the Sicangu Oyate, and that he worked as a teacher, historian, author, craftsman, and public speaker. It also notes his awards, his role at Sinte Gleska University, and his death on April 18, 2025.

SD-2026-SCSC829.s: This legislative commemoration honors the Wall Economic Development Corporation’s ten-year anniversary. It says the group was founded to support economic growth and opportunity in Wall and recognizes its work with city and community partners, including rail spur opportunities, industrial park marketing, Fly Badlands, and workforce development and leadership programs.

SD-2026-SCSC831.s: This legislative commemoration recognizes the historical significance of the buffalo and celebrates their return to tribal lands in South Dakota. It says the buffalo have long been important to the Oceti Sakowin and other tribal nations. It also says their return supports cultural renewal, ecological restoration, and future generations.

SD-2026-SJRSJR501.s: This resolution would put a constitutional amendment on the next general election ballot. The amendment would limit how long a person may serve in the South Dakota Legislature. It would allow no more than four consecutive terms or eight consecutive years in the Senate or the House, and no more than eight consecutive terms or sixteen consecutive years in the Legislature overall. Partial terms filled by appointment would not count toward these limits.

SD-2026-SJRSJR502.s: This resolution applies to Congress under Article V of the U.S. Constitution and asks for a convention to propose an amendment fixing the number of Supreme Court justices at one chief justice and eight associate justices. It directs the secretary of state to send copies to federal leaders and state legislatures. The application is meant to continue until two-thirds of the states make the same request for that purpose.

SD-2026-SJRSJR504.s: This resolution would ask voters to approve a change to the South Dakota Constitution. It would let the Legislature authorize wagering on sporting events through a mobile or electronic platform, including for people inside and outside Deadwood, if the platform is offered by or with a licensed casino and its servers are in Deadwood. The proceeds from taxes on this kind of wagering would be used for property tax relief or to reduce property taxes in this state.

SD-2026-SJRSJR505.s: This proposed constitutional amendment would be sent to voters at the next general election. It would limit the annual adjustment of the assessed value of real property and cap all ad valorem taxes on real property at one percent of assessed value. The tax cap would not apply to certain ad valorem taxes or special assessments on indebtedness approved by voters before July 1, 2028.

SD-2026-SJRSJR506.s: This joint resolution would submit a state constitutional amendment to voters at the next general election. The amendment would reset and limit ad valorem taxes on real property, with rules tied to the property’s 2027 taxes, 2020 taxes, or most recent sales price. It would affect owners of real property, and the allowed tax cap would depend on whether the owner lived in South Dakota for at least half of the previous year.

SD-2026-SJRSJR507.s: This joint resolution would submit a state law change to voters at the next general election. It would reduce certain property taxes for owner-occupied single-family homes and change several tax rates, including gross receipts taxes and use taxes. The changes would affect property owners, businesses, and people who pay the listed sales and use taxes.

SD-2026-SJRSJR508.s: This resolution would submit constitutional amendments to voters at the next general election. It would remove the lieutenant governor as the presiding officer of the Senate and repeal a provision saying the lieutenant governor shall not act as a member of the court in an impeachment trial of the governor. It would affect the structure of the state Senate and impeachment proceedings.
